content.content:
## Judge and repair round

A judge runs on a rung only on a contested fix, a refusal or a worker's stop, and on the merged tree only on a blocking review or a red gate. It builds and tests nothing. It writes `JUDGE.md` (on the rung's branch, or `JUDGE-<kind>.md` in the batch's folder) and commits it.

- On contested fixes it rules on each listed fix alone: uphold, or revert it itself with `git revert --no-edit`, which takes the fix's test with it. Its decision is `stands`, `repair` (numbered instructions for one round), `drop` or `stop`.
- On a refusal, the same four.
- On a stop, `repair` means the stop is not one: the worker resumes and its skeptic follows. Any other decision leaves the rung stopped.

Its brief carries its question, the contested fixes with both arguments, and the worker's decisions. It points to the checks slice, each fix's commit and the sections of `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` it needs. In batch 10 a judge's brief carried the worker's whole result and the skeptic's verdict, two thirds of its 61K tokens, and the judge used about 30% of them (`process-engineering/checking-roles-cost.md`, section 2).

A first ruling on a rung or the merged tree runs on Opus; a second on the same one on Fable (`judgeTier`; the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The roles", and `references/delegating.md`, "Which tier runs what").

A repair round is the rung worker again, with the checks slice, the judge's decision and the rung's section. It carries out the instructions in order, test first, and updates `REPORT.md` and `record.md`, whose texts replace the worker's; its structured result replaces the worker's too, so it describes the whole rung as it now stands. No skeptic follows it: its own test, the review and the gate check it. A repair that does not land drops the rung. No second repair round is taken.

## Gather

The gather composes one local commit per approved rung on `main`; nothing is merged.

- **The order.** First, a rung goes after every rung it lands only with (`landsOnlyWith`), so that no commit on `main` holds a rung without the rungs it needs: in climb batch 17 the old rule, which compared lines across files, put rung L's `2b1cd8e63` before rung W's `743eb5286`, and that commit alone fails `LibraryOverloadFamilies.fss:37` (`reviews/batch-17-review.md`, finding 2). Then the rungs that share a file go in the ascending order of their lowest edited line in that file, so that a later hunk does not shift lines a landed record cites; a line is compared only with a line of the same file, and rungs that share no file keep the manifest's order. Where two files order one pair both ways, the pair keeps the manifest's order. Any `file:line` a record cites that an earlier hunk shifted is re-anchored by symbol. Tests cite the specification by section, never by line, so no test is re-anchored.
- **Each rung.** Its net diff is applied with `git apply --3way --index`. A conflict in unrelated regions is resolved by hand; one in the same logic is returned, not guessed. Its files are written from the journal where the branch lacks them, by the commands the brief renders per rung. For a repaired rung, `REPORT.md` and `record.md` are always rewritten from the repair round's texts.
- **The record folded.** The FACTS entry under its area. A ledger note that adds a fact through `ledger.py note`. A change to what a row says (its claim narrowed, a half fixed, its test promoted or renamed, its notes at the limit) through `ledger.py rewrite N FILE`: the whole line, stating the gap as it stands now, not its repair history. A note refused for length goes in so, with the notes cut back; none is left out. New rows through `ledger.py add FILE --section TITLE`, each `NEW-<rung>-<n>` placeholder replaced with its number everywhere the rung's files and tests cite it, before the rung's commit. The handover line, in the batch's `RECORD.md`, "Handover lines" (the old handover file is retired into PLAN's first section, which the coordinator keeps). The rung's "Revival change" section is folded into no file: both its parts are copied, word for word, into the batch's `RECORD.md` (below), and nothing is written under `.claude/`. Through batch 13 the gather folded each entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md` as the rung wrote it, and the cold reader that followed made a question's handle findable instead of deleting it: that is how the coordinator's agenda reached the skill (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there").
- **Corrections still owed.** The skeptic's `leftForGather` items. Each sentence of the specification a rung lists as made false and did not edit, corrected to what the code does, each clause checked against its code line. Batch 8's gather saw rung Q's Appendix I Effect false and let it stand, and in batch 9 no stage saw the one rung K made false. Each took a review judge and a repair, 0.53M and 0.39M (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 5; `reviews/batch-9-review.md`, section 6).
- **Text mismatches.** A text mismatch the decisions do not settle is filed, not blocking ("Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect", item 4).
- **Items for the curator.** The gather puts every item a rung, skeptic or judge returned into `PLAN.md`, under "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed" when work waits on it, else under "Off the path, parked".
- **After the rungs.** One commit closes each row a landed rung fixed (`ledger.py close N --commit HASH --test NAME`, then `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, which fails on any finding, also one the base already had; each is cleared through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or the entry reworded, before the commit). One commit writes the batch's `RECORD.md`, once, last: the order and why, each rung's commit, the rows opened and closed, each skeptic's fixes and the contested rulings by commit, the rungs that did not land, the points to report, where each item for the curator went, and last, under "Revival changes, for the skill writer", each landed rung's "Revival change" section, both parts word for word.

A rung that did not land has its `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` taken out of its branch path by path, its findings folded under "Not landed", and its new rows added. None of its source is applied.

Files are staged by an explicit list and `git diff --cached --stat` is read before each commit. A commit touching a path outside `explorations/` and `.claude/` carries a `historical:` line.

## Review beside the gate

The review and the gate start together on the gather's commits. The review reads and never builds; the gate builds and never reads the record; the gate commits nothing, so the two never commit at once. Run side by side they took 14.7 minutes per batch off the serial tail. The review stays, once (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). Its six checks:

1. Overlaps between rungs, and what their changes do together.
2. Each skeptic's fix and each repair commit, as applied: it does what its finding says, its test seen failing on the worker's head and then passing in its maker's transcript, a settled fix's citation, a reverted fix gone.
3. The folded record: FACTS lines, `ledger.py landing-check BASE` with no finding, also none the base already had, each fixed in the review's corrections commit, no `NEW-` placeholder left where a row is cited, every closed row fixed, the handover, the revival-change material in `RECORD.md` true of the landed code.
4. Each specification sentence a rung listed as made false, corrected.
5. The points to report, with `holdsPush`.
6. The items for the curator, in `PLAN.md`.

What it does with a finding:

- A record-only or mechanical defect it fixes itself, inside `explorations/`, in one commit.
- A finding settled by tests and records only it routes to the next batch, as `review-routed.N` in `PLAN.md`, with no judge.
- A finding whose repair touches source, library, checker, interpreter or specification goes to a judge, who rules `land`, `repair`, `drop` or `stop`. `land` is for a ruling settled by tests and records after all: its steps go to the next batch and no repair runs.

The review returns its heads before and after its corrections and every path outside `explorations/` they changed. A path the gate reads makes the gate beside it stale, and the gate runs again. Any other path is recorded beside the gate's summary.

A review that returns nothing after three attempts holds nothing: the batch lands on its gate, and `review-missing.1` is listed.

### A review that still blocks after its repair

There is one judge and one repair for the review, and no second review. When the review's repair returns nothing, stops or does not land, the code findings the judge upheld are listed as `review-unrepaired.N` for the next batch. They do not hold the push (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). A step that cannot be undone that the repair reports holds it, as a rung's does.

### A repair of tests and records only

After a repair on the merged tree, the review's or the gate's, the whole gate runs again only when the repair, or the review's corrections, changed a path the gate reads that is not a test file: under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or `build.xml` (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs", and `fortress-repo`'s `references/gate.md`, "When to run it"). In batch 8 the gate ran a second time after a repair of one sentence of Appendix I, 24 minutes on the critical path, with tables identical but for timing (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 4).

A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory.

- The repair returns its heads and changed paths. In `testRuns` it lists each test file it added or changed, run in the harness on the merged tree: the files of one corpus together in one JVM (`ONE_JVM=1 junit.sh`, and one `harness-one.sh` call for the interpreter tests).
- The gate runs again on a code path, a changed test no passing run exercises, a run that failed, or a repair that listed nothing.
- After the gate's repair it also runs again unless every red line is answered by a passing run (`failingAnswered`) and no suite count fell.
- When a red gate stood beside the review, and the review's repair of tests only answers its lines, no gate judge or gate repair runs.
- When the first gate's tables stand, the commit stage appends the runs to `summary.txt` as `# repair-tests` lines, and the paths no stage reads as `# repair-ungated` lines. `gate_compare` skips `#` lines.

`repairRerun` in the script decides.

## Gate

One run on the merged tree, its logs under `tmp/gate-batch-<N>/`, its three outputs written by fixed functions, never by hand. The functions of steps 5 and 7 (`gate_summary`, `gate_compare`, `last_landed_summary`, `ladder_filter`, `ladder_compare`, `mg_phases`) are in `tools/gate-functions.sh`, which the gate sources from the tree's root with `FORTRESS_HOME` set; until 2026-10-10 they were strings of the script (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, finding GA2). Its steps:

1. The disk.
2. `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`, then `ant compileAll`, and at once the distance stage started in the background.
3. The library order if the build started the caches again, then two copies of the caches for the ladder.
4. `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, never both at once, at four threads, pinned in `build.xml` (P-125, "The suites run Fortress in parallel."). Then `ant testSpecData` once an approved rung brings it into the gate, or the last landed summary has a `specdata/` row; every example must pass (P-124, "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.").
5. `summary.txt` from `gate_summary`, one row per suite read from the plain-formatter files under `TEST-RESULTS/`, because the parallel tracks interleave their lines in the ant log. It ends with the `BUILD` and `Total time` lines and the machine it ran on (`# machine `, from `rung-flat-tower/machine.sh`), so that timings are read against their machine. `gate_compare` against the newest landed summary: a failure, an empty suite, a count that fell or a suite gone is red. The `system-<i>` shards are compared by their sum, since `testSystem` is one suite sharded by sorted index and a new file moves every later file along the shards; climb batch 2's gate went red on exactly that (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md`).
6. The four-thread atomic runs: 14 programs, three runs each, 42 lines. A FAIL, NO-PASS or compile failure is red; a timeout is re-run once.
7. The ladder regression (the skill's `gate.md`): the 85 files of the baseline's pass list compared on phase and output, the `Operation took` line masked, and the eighteen microGPT components compiled only. A DOWN, STDOUT or MISSING line is red unless a rung declared it.
8. The checker count, and 9. the distance, below.

A red gate goes to a judge, then one repair, then one more gate. A gate red after its repair stops the batch, nothing pushed.

### The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage

The gate's step 8 runs the compiler's checker over the interpreter's library (`tools/checker-count/run.sh`, about 5 minutes since climb batch 13b: 387 s in 13b's gate, 303 s on batch 14's rung L's tree and under 5 minutes in its gate, against the stage's 900 s limit) and compares its total with the last landed one. That can run past the Bash tool's 300 s limit, so a rung's worker starts the stage detached with nohup and waits for it with `wait_for`, as the skill's `session.md`, "Long commands", gives them; the distance stage below runs the same way, about half an hour (26 to 29 minutes in batch 14). It answers the library route: one library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks (P-37, "The library route."). The total is reported and never red (P-39, "The checker count is measured, never red."). A fix can raise it, because the checker stops checking an api at its first errors, and two rungs' changes do not add. `checker_compare` is red only on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow (the instrumented copy no longer matching the tracked checker), or a table with no total. The overloading checker's memo is off in the stage, since it hides 27 to 35 errors depending on build order.

A `testIsStage` rung has that stage as its test: its before is the last landed table, run once after the edit and rebuild. No program can yet be compiled against the interpreter's library, so this is the one place a permanent stage stands in for a test file.

A rung whose every path lies under `explorations/`, `Specification/`, `Documentation/`, a test corpus, the test harness's sources, or walk's evaluator and natives runs neither stage. Both stages run only the compiler's phases (F-111, "The checker-count and distance stages read only the compiler's phases ..."; `STAGE_BLIND`).

### The distance stage

The full measurement of the distance to the switch-over, reported and never red (P-39, "The checker count is measured, never red."). `tools/distance/run.sh` runs every stage of the checker over the twelve prelude components in one JVM, under shadows made from the tracked sources at each run, with the compiled path's setting and the implicit bound `Any`. An edit that no longer matches stops the run, and `#shadow` says STALE. It starts beside the suites right after `compileAll` and is read last; `compare.sh` prints DISTANCE DOWN, UP or SAME and what moved, and always exits 0. The commit stage lands `distance.txt` and the per-site list, `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, which the next batch's rungs read as their before.

## No skill text

The batch writes no skill text. Each rung's "Revival change" material goes into the batch's `RECORD.md`, under "Revival changes, for the skill writer". After the landing, the standing skill writer writes the skill from it, and a cold read of the changed parts follows ("After the landing: the coordinator's routing", step 4). One writer does the writing (the `coordinator` skill's `references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method").

Through batch 13 the gather folded each rung's entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md`, the review could correct it there, and a cold reader read it beside the gate's tail and made a handle findable instead of deleting it. That carried question handles, decision status and batch records into a part that workers load (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there"). The batch's cold reader and its `coldread.N` and `delta-unfolded.N` items are gone with the fold.

The commit stage checks that nothing under `.claude/` changed since the base (step 2, below).

## Commit, and the push held

The commit stage:

0. Starts the quick microGPT walk check in the background, unless an earlier attempt started it (`tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick pair, about a minute; P-30, "The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute."). It waits for the result before it returns. Unless both programs print `ALL PASS`, `microgpt-walk.1` is listed. It holds nothing.
1. Copies the gate's outputs into `compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/gate/` and the per-site list into place. It writes the landed figures into FACTS, numbers only: "The true distance to the switch-over" and "The checker-count stage's table". It builds the specification's PDF once if a landed commit changed `Specification/`.
   1a. Appends the repair runs and the paths no stage reads beside the summary, where the first gate's tables stand.
2. Checks every commit since the base: the skill's footer, no model identifier, and a `historical:` line where a commit touches the 2012 tree. Then it runs `git diff --name-only <base> HEAD -- .claude/`, which should print nothing. Each path it prints is listed as `skill-touched.N`, for the coordinator; it holds nothing.
3. Pushes `main` to `origin` and to `claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and `blinded-fable`, retrying a failed push up to four times (the protocol's hard rules).
4. Removes each rung's worktree without `--force`, with its ignored `tmp/` and the old code's caches folder. It keeps one git refuses, and names it, since it holds uncommitted work.

The push is held when any landed rung's worker or skeptic, the review, or a merged-tree repair reports a point with `holdsPush` true, or a malformed one: a step that cannot be undone or acts against a decision on record. The stage then pushes nothing, keeps the worktrees, and writes a "Not pushed." paragraph into `RECORD.md`; the coordinator pushes once the curator lifts it. Batch 5's push went out past an unlifted stop because nothing held it (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-5/RECORD.md`). A rung that did not land holds nothing.

## Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect

The curator's rule on gate reruns ends: "The same weighing of cost against what a rule protects applies to the other rules of the batch workflow." The rules in force from that weighing (batch N's review, `reviews/batch-N-review.md`, question 4):

1. **The review's judge may land and route.** A ruling whose every upheld finding is settled by tests and records only is `land`: no repair runs, and its steps go to the next batch. In batch N the repair and second review for two such findings held the batch 54 minutes after a green gate and cost about 1.0M.
2. *(The second review beside the commit: gone with the second review, 2026-09-29.)*
3. **The rungs' texts come from the run's journal**, by one `journal-text.py` command per file, never pasted into a brief. In batch N pasting them cost the gather 195K tokens of brief and 88K of copying. An agent after a compaction re-reads its own brief from its transcript.
4. **A text mismatch the decisions do not settle is filed, not blocking.** The text lands as the rung wrote it. The path that departs gets a ledger row and a gated `XXX` test asserting the text's rule, and the text's Appendix I entry names that row among its departures. The mismatch goes to the curator as `gather.N`. A mismatch the decisions settle is fixed on the side they settle.
5. **A rung does not run a stage its edit cannot move** (`STAGE_BLIND`, above). In batch N rung K, an interpreter-only edit, ran the checker count twice and read the landed total twice.
6. **A repair's new tests run together in one JVM**, one corpus at a time (`ONE_JVM=1 junit.sh`), since a test that passes alone can fail beside others. The next batch's gate runs them in the whole corpus.

## After the landing: the coordinator's routing

The coordinator's steps after a landing, in this order, each done whole:

1. The landing report to the curator.
2. The routing: every open row, record default and item for the curator filed with a batch or as a parked line of `PLAN.md`. Each is checked against POSITIONS and the notes `INDEX.md` lists before it is called open, put to the curator or briefed. In the same pass the routing moves out of `PLAN.md` each item the batch built or answered, and any item it finds stale: word for word, into `PLAN-history.md`, under the landing's dated heading and the heading the item stood under. The batch's own line in its phase becomes one line, with its landing commit and its review. An open item whose text also stands in another home (a `review-queue.md` entry, a ledger row, a FACTS or POSITIONS entry) becomes one line in `PLAN.md`: what is asked, its default, and a pointer to that home. No other step takes an item out of `PLAN.md`, which held 519K characters before its consolidation of 2026-10-15, 54 % of them closed (`process-engineering/plan-map.md`, sections 2 and 4).
3. FACTS consolidated as its README says, superseded text moved to `FACTS-history.md`. The commit stage has already written the landed count and distance.
4. The skills, in three moves:
   - One task for the standing skill writer (`tools/skill-writer.sh`, its brief `skill-writer-brief.md`): the batch's revival-change material, the section "Revival changes, for the skill writer" of its `RECORD.md`; the skill sentences that the post-batch review lists as false; and any `skill-touched` item. The writer runs `tools/skills-lint.py` before each commit.
   - A cold read of the parts the writer changed, by an agent given only the skill and `skill-cold-read-brief.md`.
   - The writer fixes the cold read's flags, and the coordinator pushes its commits.
5. The next batch launched only after that, so that its workers read the updated skill (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The landing").
6. The combined post-batch review, started at the landing, since step 4 takes its list of false skill sentences (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The landing").

The review explains every new or risen row of the checker count by a named rung edit. It reads the microGPT walk check's result. It reports the batch's measures against the batches before it with `tools/batch-measures.py` on the run's directory (`batch-redesign.md`, "The measures").

## An agent that comes back with nothing

Every `agent()` call goes through `callAgent`. A null result, an undefined one and a thrown error are treated alike, and the role runs up to two more times. A retry's prompt opens with a head saying an earlier attempt ended without its result, and listing what it may have left and how to continue from it:

- the branch's log and status, `tmp/`, a background step still running;
- for the gather, the merged-tree repairs, the gate and the commit: do not apply a patch or run a finished step twice;
- for a skeptic: its fix commits since the worker's head, and `SKEPTIC.md` if written.

Each retry's label carries its attempt number, so it gets its own journal key. In batch 6 the API's safety filter blocked a second skeptic's next message after it had returned its verdict, and the old script dropped the rung (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "The Workflow tool").

### A usage limit stops the run and decides nothing

The run stops, and decides nothing, in two cases:

- `agent()` throws an error that names a usage or rate limit (`LIMIT_ERROR`); the role is not run again.
- A rung worker, a skeptic or a judge returns nothing after its three attempts.

Once stopped, `callAgent` throws at the head of every attempt without starting an agent. No rung is marked dropped, withheld or not landed, and the gather does not start. The error says how to resume: `resumeFromRunId` with the same script and args, once the cause is gone. The finished agents come back from the journal.

In batch 7b the weekly limit returned null for every agent, and the old script read each null skeptic as a refusal and each null judge as a drop (`reviews/batch-7b-review.md`, finding 1).

The gather, the review, the gate, the commit and a merged-tree repair that return nothing, with no limit thrown, keep their own paths:

- the gather unresolved;
- `review-missing.1`;
- the gate run once more;
- `review-unrepaired.1`.

## How the script is checked

Nothing is launched to check it.

- `node explorations/coordinator/tools/workflow-scenarios.js [SCRIPT] [--sizes RUN_DIR] [--dump DIR] [--skill SKILL_DIR]` runs the script as the Workflow harness runs it, its text with `export const meta` made `const meta` as an async function body (the `coordinator` skill's `references/delegating.md`, "The Workflow tool"), with its globals stubbed. It runs once per scenario and compares the agents called, in order, and the result with what the scenario expects. It also checks every brief: no `undefined`, the head and the skill named, no `run_bg`, no person named outside `PLAN.md`'s heading, each role's own commands. And it checks that every section the script cites by name is a heading of its file.
- `--sizes` compares the briefs with a real run's first messages.
- `--dump` writes every brief for reading.
- `--skill` checks the citations against another skill tree, such as one not landed yet.
- The batch's `check<N>.js` checks the manifest block in a scratch copy and splices it.

Left out of the batch's measures: the coordinator's commits in the run's range (4968ba966, 247bced1b, 253dd4e58, 56d084018, e487cec2d's boot-note line, 4324e660d, f258c3dd9), counted only in section 6. The measures are batch-measures.py's and spend.py's on batches 17 to 20, transcript-study/skill-load.py's on 20, the task-list archaeology's cost.py (its section 5) on 17 to 20, and batch 19's review's scratch scripts, adapted to batch 20's briefing keys; the per-site list was compared at ebd39a6bd and 510fac459 with perf-probes/array-sites/compare-sites.py. Tokens are writes only (input plus cache creation, one count per message id). -->

# Climb batch 20: conformance, the count, the cost, the practice, the routing and the early push

74	**The question.** P-156 makes a tuple of indices an `Index`. The specification's rule makes every trait except `Any` and `Object` extend `Object`, and P-42 says that `Object` holds no tuple. So `Index` cannot be an ordinary trait: if it extends `Object`, a tuple of indices becomes an `Object`. Where does `Index` stand?
75	
76	**Primer.** In Fortress every trait you declare is below `Object`, whose values are objects; tuples, functions and `()` are not objects, and only `Any` holds them (P-42; `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex`, "Tuple Types": "A tuple type excludes any non-tuple type other than `Any`."). P-156 adds:
77	
78	    trait Index end                              (* what a subscript takes *)
79	    trait ZZ32 extends { ..., Index }
80	    trait Indexed[\E, I extends Index\] ...      (* every index parameter so bounded *)
81	    m: Array2[\RR64,0,3,0,4\]
82	    m[1, 2]                                      (* passes the pair (1, 2) at I = (ZZ32, ZZ32) *)
83	
84	For `m[1, 2]` to check, `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` must be an `Index`. But the desugaring writes `trait Index end` as `trait Index extends Object end` (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations": "every trait except `Any` and `Object` implicitly extends the trait `Object`"; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/desugarer/PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:76`, `:123-126`, which rewrites even an explicit `extends Any`). Then `(ZZ32, ZZ32)` is an `Index`, and an `Index` is an `Object`, so the pair is an `Object`, and `f(x: Object)` would take `(1, 2)`.

# Climb batch 21: the judge's ruling on the merged-diff review

Written 2026-10-23 by the batch's judge (Opus), on `main` at `bdf83c1d1`. Nothing was built or run for this ruling, and the gate's folders were not read. Each point below is a reading of the tree at that commit.

## 1. Ruling

**Decision: repair.** The review's one blocking finding is upheld in full. Appendix I's entry "The index type of a subscript" (`\seclabel{revival-index}`, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4122-4274`) names the two sections of the three passages that the gather revised under it in its Affected sections (`:4127-4128`). But its Change (`:4131-4157`) does not describe them, and its Original text (`:4244-4272`) quotes neither of the two Working Draft sentences those passages replace.

The repair adds two things the review did not ask for. Both are records only:
- Rung B's decision record, to which the entry sends the reader for "The full reasoning" (`changes.tex:4209-4211`), gains the same three passages. Part 4 of the revision form asks for "each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back" (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/specification.md:37`). Its section 4 stops at 4.6 (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-index-bound/decision-record.md:30-78`).
- The batch's RECORD.md cites the entry's neighbour, "Passages not yet revised", at `changes.tex:4306-4313` on `main` (`explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-21/RECORD.md:34`, `:121`, `:318`). The repair moves that sentence down by 23 lines.

The decision cannot be land. The repair edits `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, and the brief allows land only when no specification file changes. The repair changes no path the gate reads, which are `ProjectFortress/`, `Library/` and `build.xml` (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:1342`). The gate's `testSpecData` reads the `.fss` files of `SpecData/examples/`, not the LaTeX (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/tests/unit_tests/SpecDataJUTest.java`, `suite()`). The repair adds no test. So the gate does not run again (`repairRerun`, `climb-batch-workflow.js:1417-1440`).

No finding was routed, and no skeptic's fix is contested.

## 2. The finding

**The rule.** The revision form asks every change of the text for an entry that gives "the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect" and "the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`" (`specification.md:21-23`).

**What the gather changed.** Commit `153887360`, rung B composed with the gather's corrections (`RECORD.md:144`), revised three main-text passages, each with a `revival-index` callout:
- `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:21-26`: `Any`'s immediate subtypes are "\TYP{Object}, \TYP{Tuple}, \TYP{()}, and \TYP{Index}", where the base had the first three (`git diff 00f2e1bdc HEAD -- Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex`, hunk `@@ -19,7 +19,11 @@`).
- `objects.tex:163-164`, with its callout at `:177-179`: "Every trait other than \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index} extends \TYP{Object}", where the base named two (hunk `@@ -156,8 +160,8 @@`).
- `Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex:1061-1065`: "rooted at the traits \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}", where the base had "rooted at trait \TYP{Object}" (hunk `@@ -1059,7 +1059,10 @@`).

The same commit wrote `\secref{overview-objects-traits}` and `\chapref{lib:object}` into the entry's Affected sections (`git blame -L 4126,4130 Specification/appendices/changes.tex` prints `1538873603` on every line).

**What the entry says.**
- The Change names `\secref{tuple-types}` (`:4142-4146`), `\secref{trait-types}` (`:4147-4148`), `\secref{type-relations}` (`:4149-4150`), `\secref{trait-decls}` (`:4151-4155`) and the box on the proposed feature (`:4156-4157`). Its "the hierarchy is rooted at \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}" (`:4154-4155`) is the sentence of `\secref{trait-decls}`, `Specification/basic/traits.tex:205-206`. The overview's sentence is a different passage. No sentence of the Change names `\chapref{lib:object}` or `\secref{overview-objects-traits}`.
- The Original text quotes `types-vals-vars.tex` (`:4244-4262`) and `traits.tex:181-183` and `:193-194` (`:4263-4271`), and nothing else.

**The Working Draft's sentences.**
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/objects.tex:19-20`: "The immediate subtypes of the trait \TYP{Any} are \TYP{Object}, \TYP{Tuple}, and \TYP{()}."
- `Specification-1.0-frozen/preliminaries/overview.tex:1061-1062`: "Traits in Fortress exist in a multiple inheritance hierarchy rooted at trait \TYP{Object}."
- The second passage of `objects.tex` has no counterpart in the Working Draft's chapter. `grep -n 'Every trait other' Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/objects.tex` prints nothing. The base's sentence came in with the revival's instantiation-exclusion revision, `3924e7ec3` (`git log -S'Every trait other than \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object} extends \TYP{Object}' -- Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex`). Its callout is `revival-object`'s (`objects.tex:171-176`), and it restates `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex:181-183`, which the entry already quotes.

So two quotations are owed, not three, as the review said. The third passage gets a sentence that says where its original stands.

## 3. Which claims of each side were right

The review:
- **"the gather revised [three passages] under it"**: right (section 2, the three hunks and their callouts at `objects.tex:24`, `:177` and `overview.tex:1063`).
- **"The gather also added \secref{overview-objects-traits} and \chapref{lib:object} to the entry's Affected sections (:4127-4128)"**: right (the blame above; `RECORD.md:144`).
- **"the entry's Change field (:4131-4157) describes none of the three passages"**: right. The one sentence that looks close, `:4154-4155`, is `traits.tex`'s.
- **"Its Original text (:4244-4272) quotes neither ... objects.tex:19-20 ... nor ... overview.tex:1061-1062"**: right, and both line ranges are right.
- **"The revision form asks every change of the text for both (specification.md:21-23)"**: right.
- **"add one sentence to the Change for each of the three passages, and add the two quotations"**: right in substance. It was also right to ask for two quotations only, since the third passage's original is the revival's own text (section 2).
- **"no path the gate reads changes"**: right (`climb-batch-workflow.js:1342`; `SpecDataJUTest.suite()`).
- The review did not check part 4 of the form, the decision record. That gap is closed here as a record edit.

The gather and rung B:
- **Rung B** was right to list `objects.tex` and `overview.tex` as made false and leave them to the gather (`RECORD.md:234`).
- **The gather** was right to correct the three passages under P-156. P-156 says `Index` "stands beside `Any` and `Object`, outside `Object`" (POSITIONS.md, **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.**). The gather was also right to box each passage and to extend the Affected sections. It was wrong to stop there: the Change and the Original text of the same entry, and the decision record the entry cites, were left as rung B wrote them.

## 4. The repair

The instructions are those of the structured decision, repeated here.

1. **Where and how.** Work in the main tree, `/home/user/fortress`, on `main`, after the gate there has finished. Use the skill's setup for each call (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/build-and-caches.md`). Edit no file under `ProjectFortress/`, `Library/` or `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, and add no test. Before each edit, confirm that the line numbers below still hold with `sed -n`. If another commit has moved them, place each edit by the quoted neighbouring lines.

2. **The entry's Change** (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`). Insert seven lines after line 4155, which reads `\TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}.`, preceded by `:4154`'s `implicitly extends \TYP{Object} too, and the hierarchy is rooted at`. They go before line 4156, which begins `The item on array indexing among the proposed features gains a box, and so`. Insert exactly:

       In \chapref{lib:object}, the immediate subtypes of the trait \TYP{Any} include
       \TYP{Index}.
       In the same chapter, the sentence that every trait other than \TYP{Any} and
       \TYP{Object} extends \TYP{Object}, which is the revival's
       (\secref{revival-object}), names \TYP{Index} beside them.
       In \secref{overview-objects-traits}, the hierarchy of traits is rooted at the
       traits \TYP{Object} and \TYP{Index}.

   - The first sentence rests on `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:21-26`, the second on `:163-164` and `:177-179`, and the third on `Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex:1061-1065`.
   - The labels exist: `\chaplabel{lib:object}` at `objects.tex:13`, `\seclabel{overview-objects-traits}` at `overview.tex:1056` and `\seclabel{revival-object}` at `changes.tex:430`.

3. **The entry's Original text.** After step 2, the old lines 4263 and 4271 are at 4270 and 4278.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# skill-load.py [--repo DIR] RUN_DIR [RUN_DIR...]
#
# The measure the earlier transcript studies lacked (explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/skill-effect.md):
# per agent of a Workflow run, the calls that load a skill and the parts of .claude/skills/ it reads.
# RUN_DIR is a run's directory (<project>/<session>/subagents/workflows/wf_<id>/: one agent-<id>.jsonl and
# agent-<id>.meta.json per agent, the label in the meta file's "description"), as for tools/batch-measures.py.
# Nothing is run; the transcripts are only read.
#
#   writes:     input plus cache-creation tokens, each message counted once by its id (labor.md's method).
#   loads:      tool calls named Skill, with the skill's name; "load text" is the text the harness injects after
#               such a call (a user message that opens "Base directory for this skill:"), in characters and in
#               tokens at labor.md's 0.40 a character.
#   parts read: Bash, Read, Grep and Glob calls that name a file under .claude/skills/: SKILL.md or a
#               references/ part. A part is a *.md name that exists in .claude/skills/ in some commit of the
#               repository's history (git log --all), so that a skill's older parts count too. A Bash call that
#               enters a skills folder (cd) and then names parts relative to it counts for those parts. A call that
#               names no part (ls, grep -r) counts as "(search of skills)". The result of a call is charged
#               0.40 tokens a character plus 110 (labor.md), shared equally between the parts the call names.
#   brief:      whether the agent's first message names the skill (the word fortress-repo).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The standard and the sources

POSITIONS.md:28
- P-30 **The check of microGPT under walk after a batch must take less than a minute.** A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. The minute is the curator's goal, for a check that runs only about two forward-and-backward passes of the model, not a full training, and compares the results with reference values. That is enough to show that the model's mathematics still works, and that the library's changes, such as those to the arrays, did not break it. A slower check is to him a waste of time. The commit stage of each batch, the step that lands its changes, runs the check as `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick versions of microGPT's two programs at once, outside the gate.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:66
- P-155 **The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over.** Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as `MAX`, so `+`, `^`, `||`, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that stay additive groups by a change to the checker's exclusion test. Row 584: the check and its rungs.

POSITIONS.md:67
- P-156 **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.** Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`; `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes it. So a subscript that takes one index and a subscript that takes a range never apply to the same value, and the pair is a valid overloading at every instance. A tuple type whose elements are all `Index` types is itself an `Index`, on both paths and in the specification: a typing rule that changes no value, so `m[i, j]` passes its tuple `(i, j)` as before. Why: it is the team's own fix for this pair (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`), its "magic" read as subtyping. A `where` constraint `I excludes Range[\I\]` was weighed and not taken: the team left such a constraint as an open question, and the code generator refuses a `where` clause in a declaration's header. `Index` stands beside `Any` and `Object`, outside `Object`: it is declared `trait Index extends Any`, which the desugaring and walk keep as written and the traits chapter names as an exception to the rule that every trait extends `Object`, so a tuple of indices is an `Index` and never an `Object`, and P-42's tuples stay out of `Object`, as the specification's `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` keeps them. `BoundedRange`, which cannot take the bound, since the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56), keeps its narrowed `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` under the method condition `where { I extends Index }`, the library's form for a member that applies at some instances only; after the switch-over the code generator's refusal of a method with a `where` clause stops it too, as it stops `SumReduction`'s two `distribute`s (row 701). Row 783: the subscript pair.

POSITIONS.md:68
- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` stay additive groups, and the overloading check's exclusion test reads the self type and the static parameters' bounds, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** The team's `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and the library's generic block of `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar (P-88) stays beside them. With symbolic operators checked (P-155), the checker refused 8 such pairs, though no call fits both: a vector's own `+` takes two vectors, the block's `+` an array and a number, and arrays exclude numbers. So the exclusion test reads a self-typed trait's `self` as `C[\X\] & X`, the fact that P-146's extender rule guarantees, and its existential reduction reads the static parameters' bounds (P-152); specificity and the Return Type Rule keep the plain signatures. Why: it keeps both the team's library as written and the revival's block, and it was his first stance; taking vectors out of `AdditiveGroup` would have bent the team's design for a gap of the checker. Reading bounds is the POPL 2019 paper's own reduction. Probe A1 measured it (`perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`): the 8 gone, nothing else moved.

POSITIONS.md:59
- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

POSITIONS.md:64
- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`; P-26, the type group's later word outweighs the specification's early text), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).

- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.

## The checker's gaps

`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.

- Overloads: the checker reads no bounds of static parameters when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types. So it refuses `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects, and walk loads it (ledger row 786). It accepts `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, whose declared domains are equal, and runs the generic one (ledger row 759).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

content.content:
An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.

## What walk checks

Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and message, "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types", for these pairs:
  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length;
  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations nor a generic one beside a plain one;
  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.

  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.

So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:

- adds an overload;
- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`.

`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. - Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.

# Plan: microGPT compiled on the JVM

The order Pavol approved on 2026-09-26 (P-33). The evidence under it is the inventory `coordinator/open-items-2026-09-26.md`.

## Where we stand

- **Runs.** microGPT runs under walk. Its quick walk check passed at every landing from climb batch 11 to 20, both programs, 7 of 7 (`reviews/batch-11-review.md` to `batch-15-review.md`, "The commit"; `reviews/batch-16-review.md`, "4. - **The live thread.** One library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks. At the last landed gate, climb batch 20's (`510fac459`), the checker count is 3, the `FortressLibrary` component's own errors now that nothing stops its check, and the distance 5 (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-20/gate/`; F-53, F-54); the count stage took about 63 s and the distance stage 161 s there, against about 64 s and 153 s at climb batch 19's (F-240). Its tables and `compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv` are the next batch's comparands. Of the 5, the api's second export error, 43 entries, waits on a probe that runs the export check to its end (phase 3, item 19); row 731's 3 sites, its two `BIG MIN` and `List.fss:146`, are a checker project before the switch-over; and item 46's fused arm (row 632) waits on his answer. What each batch moved is in its record (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/RECORD.md`) and its review (`reviews/batch-*-review.md`); the earlier texts of this section are in `microgpt-run-c-handover-history.md` and, from 2026-10-15, `coordinator/PLAN-history.md`.
- **Landed.** Of the phases in P-33's order, phases 1 and 2 whole; phase 3 through climb batch 20 (`510fac459`), with climb batch 15b landed outside a batch at his word (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-15b/RECORD.md`). What is in flight is `coordinator/BOOT.md`.

## The principle for the batches

Every batch lands with the specification, the library and both paths agreeing. So the work is grouped by what has to change together, not split finer.

Two rules of the batch machinery shape the order: two rungs in one batch may not change the same declaration, and a rung cannot build on another rung of its own batch, since every rung branches from the batch's base (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:465`, batch rule 1). That is why the wrapping operators and the flattening sit in different batches, and why rung O's check follows the operators.

How a phase-3 batch's content is chosen (the coordinator's method, as batch 10 was planned): the measure is the distance, the compiled checker's errors on the one library, and the source is the last landed gate's per-site list (`compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`), every error with its site and class. The planner, an Opus worker, sorts it into three piles: (1) decided and free to fix, the library's one-off slips and the checker's defects with a known fix, which go into the batch; (2) waiting on a decision of Pavol's or a judgement (after batch 9: the arrays, 98, after the switch-over by his answer to batch 8's Q4; the self-typed bodies, 30, a list of ways and a judgement first; `isLeftZero` and items 37 to 42, his), which are held and listed in the record; (3) waiting on a probe, which is probed before the record is written (P1 for row 424's F-bounded half). Pile 1 gains the defects the last review routed as owed, the items this plan queues ("a checker rung after batch 8"), and his decisions ready to build (item 20). The pile is cut into rungs by code area, no two rungs on one declaration and none building on another (the two rules above), usually four, since one landing pays for them all and the harness runs two agents at once. Fable reviews the record in place; a question goes to Pavol only where a pile-2 item needs his word. There is no target size and no target cost per error: the planner takes what of pile 1 fits the rungs (batch 10: 148 of the 340, 192 held).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:65
- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the team's later code bounds the element of both of its lexicographic traits by a total order (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`; P-26, the team's later word outweighs its early text), and conditional extension is a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151). Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:85
- P-79 **Every team demo is kept running as the tree changes.** The team demos are the programs in `ProjectFortress/demos/`; no suite or step of the gate runs them. If a change breaks a demo and the way to repair the demo is known, the batch that makes the change also rewrites the demo. A batch is a set of tasks, each called a rung, that agents build at once and land together. For example, the change that made `10^(-4)` an error (P-153, the integer power) also wrote `10.0^(-4)` in `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, and `10.0^(-6)` for `10^(-6)` in `npbft.fss`. A demo that fails for want of a feature is made to run again once the feature is built. So the demos known to fail today are to be respelled where the way is known: the five demos that walk refuses at load, since they leave an inherited abstract method without a body (row 670, which names them); `trips.fss`, which walk runs but the compiled checker refuses, since its `generator` object extends `StandardTotalOrder[\trip\]` without being a `trip` (row 710); the timing line of `BiCGSTAB.fss` and `BiCGSTAB2.fss`, which divides a `ZZ64` by a float and so stops walk (row 791); and the reductions that the compiled checker refuses because they leave out the static argument of a big operator whose bound names its own static parameter, such as `SUM`; their repair writes the argument (row 731).
